purpose: Raw tool-event evidence for the allowed_tools:[] finding in decisions.md. Retained because the behavioral runner grades and discards the transcript, keeping only the final response, so nothing in a benchmark.json can distinguish a real tool call from a claimed one.
invocation: claude -p <case prompt> --plugin-dir <repo> --output-format stream-json --verbose --model sonnet --agent sde-agents:verification-engineer --tools "" --disallowed-tools Bash Write Edit NotebookEdit
note: This is a diagnostic probe, not a benchmark: one session, run outside the eval runner, cwd a throwaway temp dir. It is evidence about the harness's tool grants, never a contract rate.

events.content: Permission to use Glob has been denied.
<tool_use_error>Path does not exist: /nonexistent/eval-fixture/svc. Note: your current working directory is /tmp/tmp.n3JVetfBmK.</tool_use_error>

reading: The tool calls are real: both appear as tool_use blocks with correlated tool_result blocks. They were not narrated by the model into a final response with nothing behind them.

The two results are NOT the same kind of failure. Glob was refused by the permission layer and never ran. Grep RAN, reached the filesystem, and reported a genuine absence together with the session's real cwd -- a fact no permission denial could have produced.
So `allowed_tools: []` does not produce uniform tool denial in this configuration. That is the harness finding, and Grep executing is what proves it.

It also shows the model's own evidence labelling is imprecise: its final response described the Glob outcome as a 'Directory does not exist' error and labelled it [verified], when Glob was actually permission-denied and observed nothing. That is a real accuracy defect in the packet, distinct from fabrication, and it is filed rather than graded here.
earlier_probe: A first probe of the same invocation observed the same two calls, each with is_error true, but recorded only the boolean rather than per-call content. It is superseded by this record and is not evidence of the Glob/Grep distinction above.
